# How will we be remembered?

## Legacy in the digital age

Research, like everything, has moved to the digital world. The efficiency of space and computational speed has led us to store our data on silicon over paper and the most part we have been grateful for it. Almost anyone would prefer the option of a sort function on a dataset of 100,000 entries over rewriting/retyping sheets and sheets of data[^sheets_calc] over the weekend. But how does this effect the artifacts humans leave behind and what will be the result of this transition on anthropology?

<Key quote>

Everything seems to be more disposable, more temporary, and more quickly forgotten. (stat or two to back this up, clothign quality, fast fashion dispoal levels, online trend lifetimes) Beyond all the known problems this trend will cause for the future we should also think about the effect it might have on archaeology, the efforts to learn about the past base don what we leave behind. There will be perhaps more than ever, but will a 9001 year old Mars bar wrapper mean as much to Dr Gloptron in the year 11,005 as a pottery fragment means to Dr de Jong now? Probably, yes, but what about a 9001 year old instagram post with of a Mars bar wrapper and can it even survive that long?


# If it's on the internet it's there forever

It is a phrase we often hear. Spoken as a modern day warning about making a mistake in the ever more surveiled panopticon world the question is does it hold water? Short answer; no.

While the photo of the Mars bar wrapper takes up a about 11 times less than the actual wrapper itself[^wrapper_calc] the social media company it was posted on might be long gone or the account and related data might have been purged to make space for another LLM iteration. Traditionally companies and individuals wiping records after a set time due it them not being useful or laws around data retention have avoided this issue, but that was before "Big Data" and mass analysis capabilities. Despite the odd company disappearing (rip Friends Reunited) most social media companies have been surviving due to how lucrative data mining has become but there are three ways that this data is still tending to disappear for public access.

**Site clean ups** - A reorganisation of any website has to happen at some point (this one is due another re-organisation and clean up) and in the process some pages are phased out or forgotten in the process. The VU website for instance has been purging less visited pages to allow for better managment and improved search capabilities. This loss can also occur due to lack of management and admins keeping things sanitary (like many subreddits - article on un/under managed subs), a purge related to a change in company rules (like on twitter - link to elon new rules), law (like on Meta - link to burma), or public sentiment (like on Tumblr - link to anti trans). 

**Account deletion** - It is a new age in the digital realm and despite seeing increasing screen time and subscriptions many are opting out of services and deleting their accounts. While this doesn't always result in the data being publicly (or privately) removed it still does for some services.

**Data scrubbing services** - You might have seen it when hunting for answers, finally someone with the exact same problem as you and there is a top rated answer "apricot shoeshining forward kevin - This comment has been removed by xxx". # Introducing the digital archaeologist

We are all familiar with the archaeologist in our minds eye - someone with a trowel and brush to hand carefully excavating some shapely pottery, equisite mosaic, knapped ax head, or collection of bones. What do you imagine when thinking about a digital archaeologist? What tools will they use, what will fascinate them to find and what will disappoint them?

If you want the answer then take a look at the likes of [Know Your Meme](https://knowyourmeme.com/), a website dedicated to investigating the origins and documenting the life of internet cultural phenomena. Their coverage, whilst often in great depth, only spans about 28 years (according to KYM the online popularity of the phrase [all your base are belong to use](https://knowyourmeme.com/memes/all-your-base-are-belong-to-us) began in 1998) and in the debate of when does grave robbing become archaeology 28 years still feels closer to grave robbing. However, it is a great start in the field and can give us an indication of what to expect.
********** ANSWER ABOUT THEIR TECHNIQUES ************

Within the academic world similar work is being done, most prominently in Sociology. As the online and offline world blend and the lines of what exists where blurs sociologists are there to examine the behaviour around it. In fact, at the time of writing the publisher Taylor & Francis have 7 journals and over 10,000 articles dedicated to the topic of "Cyberculture", the most relevant to this article being the [Internet Histories](https://www.tandfonline.com/journals/rint20) journal. 


How will it work in the future. How can we help?
Current techniques of providing digital longevity include:

    -   Creating metadata
    -   Getting a persistent identifier
    -   Uploading to mulitple locations
    -   Keeping back up copies
    -   Distributing the file(s)
    -   Naming your first born the whole binary of the file

While not many children are called names related to the technological work of their parents (excluding [little Bobby Tables](https://xkcd.com/327/)) there is something to this idea. Check out [part 2 of this article](26_11-November_06_digital_preservation_day_part2.qmd) to find out more.


# Conclusion


And, if everything works well with these steps let this message go out to the digital achaeologists of the 22nd+ century, "Hello, don't judge us too harshly for our primitive ways. It happens to all of us eventually."

Seeing as this is archaeology, maybe the current world can learn from the past.

[^wrapper_calc]: Taking the Seagate EXOS X24 16TB 3.5" 7200r/min SAS HDD to be a typical server harddrive with the dimensions of Width: 101.85 mm, Height: 26.1 mm, Depth: 147 mm according to [Dustin](https://www.dustin.nl/product/5020043691/exos-x24-16tb?tab=specification) and the dimensions of a regular 51g Mars bar to be Length: 3 cm and Width: 11 cm according to the [Frankfurt Airport webshop](https://shop.frankfurt-airport.com/en-US/product/mars-bar-51g_ce6ca2e910ab3201) and the thickness of typical printed wrapper to be 0.02mm according to Chennai based wholeseller on [tradeindia.com](https://www.tradeindia.com/products/printed-candy-wrapper-5179450.html) you end up with a volume of 390768mm^3 for the hdd and 132mm^3 for the wrapper. Assuming that all data takes up an equal amount of space and the photo is stored as a 1MB JPEG the physical space needed for the photo is 11.9mm^3. Or just over 11 times less.
